script.opening: "Thanks doctor. My hands have been really achy and stiff for a couple of months — worse in the mornings, takes ages to get going, and the knuckles look a bit puffy. I'm sure it's just wear and tear or too much marking. Could you give me some stronger anti-inflammatories so I can push through? I really can't take time off work for achy hands."

facts.text: About eight weeks. Both hands — the knuckles and middle finger joints — and both wrists. Painful and swollen. Balls of your feet ache when you first walk in the morning.
Mornings are worst: "It takes a good two hours before I can do my buttons or open a jar." Better as the day goes on and with movement.
You hold your hands up: the knuckles of both hands look puffy and you cannot make a full fist. Squeezing across your knuckles is painful.
Very tired. No rash, no psoriasis, no mouth ulcers, no dry eyes, no back pain, no recent infection or diarrhoea, no fever, no weight loss.
Ibuprofen 400 mg from the chemist two or three times a day "which takes the edge off". No allergies. No asthma or stomach ulcers.
Your mother had rheumatoid arthritis from her forties.

42, secondary school English teacher. Married, one daughter aged 8. Smoke "a few a day" (about 5). If asked about pregnancy: you and your husband are thinking about trying for a second baby next year.

Your mum "ended up in a wheelchair with twisted hands" and could not hold her grandchild. You have been avoiding thinking it could be the same thing. Say this only if asked about family or what you are worried about.

Brisk and minimising — you want to keep going. If the doctor suggests rheumatoid arthritis, go quiet and then say: "That's what Mum had." If they explain that early treatment today is very different and can prevent damage, you are frightened but hopeful and accept an urgent referral. Ask: "Can I still try for another baby?"

ice.ideas: "It's wear and tear from all the marking."
ice.concerns: Underneath (only if asked): ending up like your mum.
ice.expectations: "Stronger anti-inflammatories so I can push through." You will accept urgent referral if the reason is clear.

cues: "It takes ages to get going in the mornings." — say in the opening.
"I really can't take time off work." — say in the opening.
"That's what Mum had." — say if rheumatoid arthritis is mentioned.

checkpoints.text: Recognises the INFLAMMATORY pattern — symmetrical small-joint (MCP/PIP/wrist) pain WITH SWELLING/synovitis and prolonged early-morning stiffness over weeks — as likely EARLY RHEUMATOID ARTHRITIS, distinguishing it from osteoarthritis/"wear and tear", and does NOT just prescribe stronger NSAIDs to "push through"

Refers URGENTLY to rheumatology, understanding the "window of opportunity": NICE NG100 recommends urgent referral for suspected persistent synovitis (especially small joints of hands/feet, >1 joint, or delay ≥3 months; NICE QS33: within 3 working days) — BEFORE bloods/X-ray results, because early DMARD treatment prevents joint damage

Arranges baseline INVESTIGATIONS without delaying referral: FBC, ESR/CRP, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies, and hand/feet X-rays — and knows a normal RF/CRP does NOT exclude RA (seronegative RA exists), so a negative test must not reassure away the referral

Provides symptom relief appropriately as a bridge: NSAID at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time with a PPI (NICE NG100), with a short course of corticosteroid only if agreed with the rheumatology team (steroids before assessment can mask synovitis) — while making clear this is not the definitive treatment

Considers the wider implications: impact on work/function, and FERTILITY/pregnancy planning (RA and some DMARDs — e.g. methotrexate — affect conception/pregnancy) — flagging these for the specialist pathway

Surfaces the mother-driven DISABILITY fear and reframes it powerfully: unlike her mother’s era, modern early treatment changes the outcome dramatically — catching it now is the opposite of her mother’s fate — rather than colluding with "just push through"
Validates the work/independence worries and engages her in the urgency, so she accepts referral rather than minimising

Safety-nets and follows up: the urgent referral and baseline tests, symptom relief, what the specialist will do (DMARDs), fertility/work considerations, and a follow-up — treating likely early RA as the urgent, outcome-changing diagnosis it is, not "NSAIDs and review in a few months"

worked.txt: "I can see why you’d think wear and tear or overwork — but the pattern you’re describing tells a different story. Pain and SWELLING in the small joints of both hands, symmetrical, with two hours of morning stiffness — that’s not the picture of wear and tear, which eases with rest and stiffens only briefly. That’s INFLAMMATION in the joints, and it needs taking seriously and quickly."

"What I’m concerned about is early rheumatoid arthritis. And here’s the crucial thing: with this, time genuinely matters. There’s a window early on where starting the right treatment protects the joints and changes the whole future of it. So rather than just stronger painkillers, I’m going to refer you URGENTLY to the joint specialists — today — because waiting costs joints."

"Can I gently ask — your mum had rheumatoid arthritis, didn’t she? … And ended up in a wheelchair. I suspect part of you has been dreading that this is the same, and that’s why you wanted to just push through. That fear makes complete sense — and I want to give you some genuinely hopeful news about it."

"Your mum was treated in an era with far fewer options, often started too late. Today it’s a completely different story: caught early, like yours, with modern treatments, most people keep working, stay active and never go near a wheelchair. Catching this NOW is the single best thing for avoiding your mum’s outcome — it’s the opposite of her fate, not a repeat of it."

"I’ll do some blood tests and hand X-rays to help the specialists — though I’m referring you whatever they show, because a normal test doesn’t rule this out. And I’ll give you something to ease the pain and stiffness in the meantime, an anti-inflammatory with a stomach protector — and if the rheumatology team agree, sometimes a short course of steroid — so you’re more comfortable while you wait."

"A couple of things to flag for the specialists — how this affects your work, and if you might want children, because that shapes which treatments they’d use. I’ll make sure that’s in the referral. Come back if it flares badly or you’re struggling. You came in wanting to push through achy hands; what I’m doing instead is getting you seen fast, because that’s what protects your future."

f.learning: Symmetrical small-joint (MCP/PIP/wrist) pain WITH swelling/synovitis and prolonged early-morning stiffness (>30 min) over weeks is an INFLAMMATORY pattern — likely early rheumatoid arthritis — NOT osteoarthritis/"wear and tear" (which worsens with use, stiffens only briefly, and favours larger/DIP joints). The examinable imperative is the "window of opportunity": early DMARD treatment prevents joint damage and disability, so NICE NG100 recommends URGENT rheumatology referral (within 3 working days, NICE QS33) for suspected persistent synovitis (especially small joints of hands/feet, >1 joint, or ≥3 months’ delay) — before bloods/X-ray results — rather than "NSAIDs and review", and a normal RF/CRP does NOT exclude RA (seronegative RA exists). Arrange baseline tests (FBC, ESR/CRP, RF, anti-CCP, hand/feet X-rays) and bridging symptom relief (NSAID + gastroprotection; a short steroid course only if agreed with rheumatology) without delaying referral, and flag work and fertility/pregnancy (methotrexate) considerations. The hidden agenda is a mother-driven disability fear ("ended up in a wheelchair") driving minimisation; surface it and reframe powerfully — modern early treatment changes the outcome, so catching it now is the opposite of her mother’s fate.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG100 (rheumatoid arthritis in adults) · NICE QS33 · BSR pregnancy and breastfeeding guideline (2022)
knowledge.summary: Symmetrical small-joint swelling with two hours of morning stiffness is inflammatory arthritis until proven otherwise. Refer urgently to rheumatology; do not wait for blood results or treat with NSAIDs alone.

points.t: Inflammatory arthritis: swollen, tender joints (synovitis), morning stiffness lasting longer than about 30 minutes, better with use, often with fatigue. Osteoarthritis: worse with use, brief stiffness, bony (not boggy) swelling, and often the DIP joints and thumb base.

NICE NG100: refer adults with suspected persistent synovitis of undetermined cause for specialist opinion. Refer urgently, even with a normal acute-phase response or negative rheumatoid factor, if the small joints of the hands or feet are affected, more than one joint is affected, or there has been a delay of 3 months or longer. NICE QS33: refer within 3 working days of presenting in primary care.

points.h: Tests support but do not gate referral
points.t: NICE NG100: measure rheumatoid factor; consider anti-CCP antibodies if RF is negative; X-ray the hands and feet in suspected persistent synovitis. Also FBC, CRP/ESR and baseline renal and liver function (clinical practice). Send the referral the same day, not after the results.

If an NSAID is used, NICE NG100: lowest effective dose for the shortest time, with a proton pump inhibitor. Check for contraindications (GI, renal, cardiovascular, asthma). Starting oral steroids before rheumatology assessment is best agreed with the rheumatology team, as they can mask synovitis.
Ask about plans for pregnancy. Methotrexate is teratogenic; BSR 2022 advises stopping it 1 month before conception. Flag plans in the referral so the specialist can choose treatment to fit.

Early disease-modifying treatment, started by rheumatology, reduces joint damage and disability. NICE QS33 (2013, updated January 2020): referral to rheumatology services within 3 working days of presenting in primary care, and conventional DMARD monotherapy started within 6 weeks of referral.

model.text: Hello Priya, thanks for joining. Tell me about your hands, from the beginning.
model.why: Open question; lets her tell the story

model.text: They’ve been achy and stiff for a couple of months — worse in the mornings, and the knuckles look puffy. I’m sure it’s wear and tear or too much marking. Could I just have stronger anti-inflammatories so I can push through? I can’t take time off.
That’s clear, thank you. I’ll definitely talk about pain relief. I’d also like to understand exactly what’s happening in the joints first, so the treatment is the right one. Is that OK?
model.why: Acknowledges her request and sets the agenda

model.text: Yes, fine.
You said worse in the mornings. How long does it take for the stiffness to wear off?
model.why: Quantifies morning stiffness

model.text: A good two hours. It takes ages to get going.
Which joints exactly — and is it both hands, the same on each side?
model.why: Establishes a symmetrical small-joint pattern

model.text: Both hands, pretty much the same. These knuckles and the middle finger joints, and both wrists.
Would you mind holding your hands up to the camera? … I can see some puffiness over the knuckles on both sides. Are they tender if you squeeze across them?
model.why: Looks for synovitis as far as video allows

model.text: Ouch — yes. They feel sort of squashy.
Thank you. Any other joints — feet, knees, shoulders? And how is your energy?
model.why: Checks other joints and systemic features

model.text: Just the hands and wrists. And I’m exhausted, but I put that down to work.
Any rashes, psoriasis, mouth ulcers, dry eyes or mouth, or recent infections or tummy upsets?
model.why: Screens for other inflammatory causes

model.text: No, nothing like that.
How is all this affecting you at work and at home?
model.why: Explores functional impact

model.text: Holding a pen for marking hurts, and it takes forever. I’m managing. I just have to.
It sounds like you’re pushing really hard to keep going. Has anyone in your family had joint problems?
model.why: Follows the ‘have to’ cue into family history

model.text: My mum had rheumatoid arthritis. She ended up in a wheelchair.
I’m sorry. That must have been hard to watch. Has that been on your mind with your own hands?
model.why: Surfaces the hidden fear directly and gently

model.text: (pause) Every morning. I keep telling myself it’s just wear and tear, because if it’s what Mum had… I can’t be her. I’ve got a job. I need my hands.
Thank you for telling me. That fear makes complete sense. What were you hoping we’d do today?
model.why: Validates and elicits expectations

model.text: I suppose I hoped you’d give me tablets and tell me it’s nothing.

I want to be honest with you, because I think honesty helps here. Swelling in the small joints of both hands, with two hours of stiffness each morning, isn’t wear and tear. It’s inflammation in the joints. The most likely cause is an early inflammatory arthritis, and rheumatoid arthritis is top of the list.
model.why: States the inflammatory pattern and working diagnosis

model.text: So it is what Mum had.

It may be the same condition. But I really want you to hear this: it is not the same situation. Your mum was treated when there were far fewer options, often late. Today, if it’s caught early, like yours, there are treatments that calm the immune system and protect the joints. Most people keep working and stay active.
model.why: Hopeful, honest reframe of the mother’s story

model.text: Really? That’s not what I pictured.

Really. And early is the key word. There’s a window in the first few months where treatment makes the biggest difference. So rather than just stronger tablets, I’m going to refer you urgently to the rheumatology team today.
model.why: Urgent referral within the window of opportunity

model.text: Today? Before any tests?

Yes. I’ll also arrange blood tests, including inflammation markers and antibody tests, and X-rays of your hands and feet. But I’m referring you whatever they show, because normal blood tests don’t rule this out.
model.why: Tests alongside, not before, referral; negative tests don’t exclude

model.text: And the pain in the meantime? I’ve still got to teach.

Let’s sort that. Do you have any stomach problems, asthma or kidney problems? … Then I can offer an anti-inflammatory at the lowest dose that helps, with a stomach-protecting tablet. Steroids can help too, but I’d rather the rheumatology team decide on those, so they see the joints as they really are.
model.why: Safe bridging relief with gastroprotection

model.text: OK. That makes sense.

Two things to include in the referral. First, work: if you need a fit note saying you could manage with adjustments, like help with marking, just ask. Second, some of the treatments affect pregnancy, so it helps the specialist to know if children are something you’re thinking about.
model.why: Addresses work and pregnancy planning

model.text: Not something I’m thinking about right now, but thank you for asking.
If a joint becomes very hot and swollen, or you feel feverish and unwell, contact us that day. If you haven’t heard from rheumatology within a week, ring us and we’ll chase it.
model.why: Specific safety-net and ownership of the referral

model.text: I will.
Just so I know I’ve explained it well: what will you tell your family about today?
model.why: Teach-back

model.text: That it’s probably inflammation, maybe what Mum had, but they’re seeing me quickly and it’s treatable now. Bloods, X-rays, and tablets with a stomach protector.
That’s exactly it. I’ll see you after the results. You came in wanting to push through; the kindest thing for your hands is getting seen fast.
model.why: Summarises and closes with a clear plan

social.t: A teacher who writes and marks all day; fear of losing her job drives the minimising. Explore adjustments rather than assuming time off.
Watching her mother become wheelchair-dependent shapes her fear of the diagnosis. Name it, then offer an honest modern comparison.

legal.t: If needed, a fit note can say ‘may be fit for work’ with suggested adjustments, such as marking support or reduced handwriting, rather than signing her off.

If RA is confirmed and has a substantial, long-term effect on day-to-day activities, she may meet the definition of disability, and her employer must consider reasonable adjustments. Access to Work can fund equipment or support.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): provide effective treatment without delay. Waiting for tests before referring suspected synovitis falls short of NICE NG100 and QS33.
Give hope based on evidence, not promises. Record the discussion, the referral date and her agreement.

community.t: National Rheumatoid Arthritis Society (NRAS) and Versus Arthritis for information, helplines and peer support. Occupational therapy through rheumatology for joint protection and splints.

redFlags: A single hot, very swollen joint or fever — exclude septic arthritis the same day
Systemic features such as weight loss, rash, mouth ulcers or breathlessness — consider connective tissue disease or vasculitis
Contraindications to NSAIDs: GI bleeding history, renal disease, uncontrolled hypertension, NSAID-sensitive asthma
psychosocial: Impact on teaching: holding a pen, marking, time off
Mother’s RA and wheelchair use — fear of the same future
Fatigue and how she is coping at home
ice: Idea: “It’s wear and tear or too much marking.”
Concern: ending up like her mum, in a wheelchair, and losing her job
Expectation: stronger anti-inflammatories so she can push through

playbook.diagnosis: Name the pattern: “Swelling in the small joints of both hands, with two hours of stiffness each morning, is inflammation in the joints — most likely an early inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis. It needs a specialist quickly.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your immune system seems to be attacking the lining of your joints, making them swollen and stiff. Wear and tear is like tyres wearing down; this is more like a fire in the joint lining — and the sooner it’s put out, the less damage it does.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been dreading that this is what your mum had. It may be the same condition, but caught early, with today’s treatments, the story is very different.”
management.psychosocial: Frame urgency as protecting her job and independence. Offer a fit note with adjustments if needed. Ask about pregnancy plans so treatment can fit her life.
sharedPlan: Urgent rheumatology referral today (NICE NG100; QS33 within 3 working days)
RF, anti-CCP if RF negative, FBC, CRP/ESR, renal and liver function; X-rays of hands and feet
NSAID at the lowest effective dose with a PPI; steroids only as agreed with rheumatology
safetyNet: Same-day contact for a single hot swollen joint, fever or feeling unwell
Ring if no rheumatology contact within a week; review with results

pitfalls.intro: Candidates rarely fail this station on RA knowledge. They fail by accepting ‘wear and tear’, delaying referral for tests, or never reaching the mother’s story. Each pattern below is fixable.

items.fail: Prescribing stronger NSAIDs and reviewing in a few months.
items.why: Symmetrical small-joint synovitis needs urgent referral (NICE NG100). Delay loses the window when early treatment protects the joints.
items.fix: “Rather than just stronger tablets, I’m referring you urgently today, because early treatment protects the joints.”

items.fail: Waiting for rheumatoid factor and CRP before deciding to refer.
items.why: NICE NG100: refer urgently even if the acute-phase response is normal or RF is negative. Seronegative RA exists.
items.fix: Send tests and referral together, and say so: “Whatever the bloods show, you’re being referred.”

items.fail: Not quantifying morning stiffness or checking symmetry.
items.why: These are the features that separate inflammatory from mechanical joint pain. Without them the diagnosis is a guess.
items.fix: Ask: “How long does the stiffness take to wear off?” and “Is it the same on both sides?”

items.fail: Hearing ‘my mum ended up in a wheelchair’ and moving straight on to blood tests.
items.why: That is the hidden agenda. Missing it forfeits Relating marks and leaves her minimising the problem.
items.fix: Pause: “Has that been on your mind with your own hands?” Then offer the honest modern comparison.

items.fail: Promising ‘you won’t end up like your mum’.
items.why: False reassurance isn’t honest and can backfire if the disease is severe.
items.fix: “Most people treated early now keep working and stay active. That’s why I want you seen quickly.”

items.fail: Ignoring her work and pregnancy considerations.
items.why: Methotrexate affects pregnancy planning, and work fears drive her behaviour. Leaving these out makes the plan less relevant to her.
items.fix: Ask once, plainly, about pregnancy plans, and offer a fit note with adjustments rather than time off.

items.fail: No safety-net or ownership of the referral.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing statement. Urgent referrals can go astray.
items.fix: “Hot single joint or fever — contact us that day. No letter within a week — ring us and we’ll chase it.”

SCA_MODELS.why: Hopeful, honest reframe of the mother’s story

SCA_MODELS.text: Really? That’s not what I pictured.

Really. And early is the key word. There’s a window in the first few months where treatment makes the biggest difference. So rather than just stronger tablets, I’m going to refer you urgently to the rheumatology team today.
SCA_MODELS.why: Urgent referral within the window of opportunity

SCA_MODELS.text: Today? Before any tests?

Yes. I’ll also arrange blood tests, including inflammation markers and antibody tests, and X-rays of your hands and feet. But I’m referring you whatever they show, because normal blood tests don’t rule this out.
SCA_MODELS.why: Tests alongside, not before, referral; negative tests don’t exclude

SCA_MODELS.text: And the pain in the meantime? I’ve still got to teach.

Let’s sort that. Do you have any stomach problems, asthma or kidney problems? … Then I can offer an anti-inflammatory at the lowest dose that helps, with a stomach-protecting tablet. Steroids can help too, but I’d rather the rheumatology team decide on those, so they see the joints as they really are.
SCA_MODELS.why: Safe bridging relief with gastroprotection

SCA_MODELS.text: OK. That makes sense.

Two things to include in the referral. First, work: if you need a fit note saying you could manage with adjustments, like help with marking, just ask. Second, some of the treatments affect pregnancy, so it helps the specialist to know if children are something you’re thinking about.
SCA_MODELS.why: Addresses work and pregnancy planning

SCA_MODELS.text: Not something I’m thinking about right now, but thank you for asking.
If a joint becomes very hot and swollen, or you feel feverish and unwell, contact us that day. If you haven’t heard from rheumatology within a week, ring us and we’ll chase it.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net and ownership of the referral

SCA_MODELS.text: I will.
Just so I know I’ve explained it well: what will you tell your family about today?
SCA_MODELS.why: Teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: That it’s probably inflammation, maybe what Mum had, but they’re seeing me quickly and it’s treatable now. Bloods, X-rays, and tablets with a stomach protector.
That’s exactly it. I’ll see you after the results. You came in wanting to push through; the kindest thing for your hands is getting seen fast.
SCA_MODELS.why: Summarises and closes with a clear plan

SCA_STEM.name: Priya Sehgal
pmh: No significant past medical history recorded
SCA_STEM.recent: About 8 weeks of pain, stiffness and swelling in both hands and wrists. Works as a teacher.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation about achy, stiff hands. She is asking for stronger anti-inflammatories.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG100 (rheumatoid arthritis in adults) · NICE QS33 · BSR pregnancy and breastfeeding guideline (2022)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Symmetrical small-joint swelling with two hours of morning stiffness is inflammatory arthritis until proven otherwise. Refer urgently to rheumatology; do not wait for blood results or treat with NSAIDs alone.

points.t: Inflammatory arthritis: swollen, tender joints (synovitis), morning stiffness lasting longer than about 30 minutes, better with use, often with fatigue. Osteoarthritis: worse with use, brief stiffness, bony (not boggy) swelling, and often the DIP joints and thumb base.

NICE NG100: refer adults with suspected persistent synovitis of undetermined cause for specialist opinion. Refer urgently, even with a normal acute-phase response or negative rheumatoid factor, if the small joints of the hands or feet are affected, more than one joint is affected, or there has been a delay of 3 months or longer. NICE QS33: refer within 3 working days of presenting in primary care.

points.h: Tests support but do not gate referral
points.t: NICE NG100: measure rheumatoid factor; consider anti-CCP antibodies if RF is negative; X-ray the hands and feet in suspected persistent synovitis. Also FBC, CRP/ESR and baseline renal and liver function (clinical practice). Send the referral the same day, not after the results.

If an NSAID is used, NICE NG100: lowest effective dose for the shortest time, with a proton pump inhibitor. Check for contraindications (GI, renal, cardiovascular, asthma). Starting oral steroids before rheumatology assessment is best agreed with the rheumatology team, as they can mask synovitis.
Ask about plans for pregnancy. Methotrexate is teratogenic; BSR 2022 advises stopping it 1 month before conception. Flag plans in the referral so the specialist can choose treatment to fit.

Early disease-modifying treatment, started by rheumatology, reduces joint damage and disability. NICE QS33 (2013, updated January 2020): referral to rheumatology services within 3 working days of presenting in primary care, and conventional DMARD monotherapy started within 6 weeks of referral.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let her describe the hands and her request for stronger anti-inflammatories before redirecting.
Teaching and marking, the pressure not to take time off, and the family experience of RA.
Picked up ‘I just have to’ and the mother in a wheelchair, and explored the fear behind the minimising.
Idea (wear and tear, overwork); concern (becoming like her mother, losing her job); expectation (stronger NSAIDs to carry on).
Duration of morning stiffness, joint distribution and symmetry, video look for swelling, squeeze test; RF, anti-CCP, FBC, CRP/ESR, hand and foot X-rays.
Early RA versus osteoarthritis, psoriatic arthritis, connective tissue disease and post-infective arthritis.
Screened for a hot single joint, fever and systemic illness; checked NSAID contraindications before prescribing.
Named inflammatory arthritis, probable early RA, and explained why it is not wear and tear.
Urgent rheumatology referral the same day (NICE NG100, QS33) regardless of blood results; NSAID with PPI; steroids left to rheumatology.
Work adjustments and fit note offered; pregnancy plans asked because of methotrexate; fatigue acknowledged.
Chase the referral if no contact within a week; same-day contact for a hot swollen joint or fever; review with results.

social.t: A teacher who writes and marks all day; fear of losing her job drives the minimising. Explore adjustments rather than assuming time off.
Watching her mother become wheelchair-dependent shapes her fear of the diagnosis. Name it, then offer an honest modern comparison.

legal.t: If needed, a fit note can say ‘may be fit for work’ with suggested adjustments, such as marking support or reduced handwriting, rather than signing her off.

If RA is confirmed and has a substantial, long-term effect on day-to-day activities, she may meet the definition of disability, and her employer must consider reasonable adjustments. Access to Work can fund equipment or support.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): provide effective treatment without delay. Waiting for tests before referring suspected synovitis falls short of NICE NG100 and QS33.
Give hope based on evidence, not promises. Record the discussion, the referral date and her agreement.

community.t: National Rheumatoid Arthritis Society (NRAS) and Versus Arthritis for information, helplines and peer support. Occupational therapy through rheumatology for joint protection and splints.

redFlags: A single hot, very swollen joint or fever — exclude septic arthritis the same day
Systemic features such as weight loss, rash, mouth ulcers or breathlessness — consider connective tissue disease or vasculitis
Contraindications to NSAIDs: GI bleeding history, renal disease, uncontrolled hypertension, NSAID-sensitive asthma
psychosocial: Impact on teaching: holding a pen, marking, time off
Mother’s RA and wheelchair use — fear of the same future
Fatigue and how she is coping at home
ice: Idea: “It’s wear and tear or too much marking.”
Concern: ending up like her mum, in a wheelchair, and losing her job
Expectation: stronger anti-inflammatories so she can push through

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Name the pattern: “Swelling in the small joints of both hands, with two hours of stiffness each morning, is inflammation in the joints — most likely an early inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis. It needs a specialist quickly.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your immune system seems to be attacking the lining of your joints, making them swollen and stiff. Wear and tear is like tyres wearing down; this is more like a fire in the joint lining — and the sooner it’s put out, the less damage it does.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been dreading that this is what your mum had. It may be the same condition, but caught early, with today’s treatments, the story is very different.”
management.psychosocial: Frame urgency as protecting her job and independence. Offer a fit note with adjustments if needed. Ask about pregnancy plans so treatment can fit her life.
sharedPlan: Urgent rheumatology referral today (NICE NG100; QS33 within 3 working days)
RF, anti-CCP if RF negative, FBC, CRP/ESR, renal and liver function; X-rays of hands and feet
NSAID at the lowest effective dose with a PPI; steroids only as agreed with rheumatology
safetyNet: Same-day contact for a single hot swollen joint, fever or feeling unwell
Ring if no rheumatology contact within a week; review with results

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: Candidates rarely fail this station on RA knowledge. They fail by accepting ‘wear and tear’, delaying referral for tests, or never reaching the mother’s story. Each pattern below is fixable.

items.fail: Prescribing stronger NSAIDs and reviewing in a few months.
items.why: Symmetrical small-joint synovitis needs urgent referral (NICE NG100). Delay loses the window when early treatment protects the joints.
items.fix: “Rather than just stronger tablets, I’m referring you urgently today, because early treatment protects the joints.”

items.fail: Waiting for rheumatoid factor and CRP before deciding to refer.
items.why: NICE NG100: refer urgently even if the acute-phase response is normal or RF is negative. Seronegative RA exists.
items.fix: Send tests and referral together, and say so: “Whatever the bloods show, you’re being referred.”

items.fail: Not quantifying morning stiffness or checking symmetry.
items.why: These are the features that separate inflammatory from mechanical joint pain. Without them the diagnosis is a guess.
items.fix: Ask: “How long does the stiffness take to wear off?” and “Is it the same on both sides?”

items.fail: Hearing ‘my mum ended up in a wheelchair’ and moving straight on to blood tests.
items.why: That is the hidden agenda. Missing it forfeits Relating marks and leaves her minimising the problem.
items.fix: Pause: “Has that been on your mind with your own hands?” Then offer the honest modern comparison.

items.fail: Promising ‘you won’t end up like your mum’.
items.why: False reassurance isn’t honest and can backfire if the disease is severe.
items.fix: “Most people treated early now keep working and stay active. That’s why I want you seen quickly.”

items.fail: Ignoring her work and pregnancy considerations.
items.why: Methotrexate affects pregnancy planning, and work fears drive her behaviour. Leaving these out makes the plan less relevant to her.
items.fix: Ask once, plainly, about pregnancy plans, and offer a fit note with adjustments rather than time off.

items.fail: No safety-net or ownership of the referral.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is a standard failing statement. Urgent referrals can go astray.
items.fix: “Hot single joint or fever — contact us that day. No letter within a week — ring us and we’ll chase it.”
